name: NPUs and TPUs
blurb: Purpose-built accelerators outside the GPU line.

items.name: Neural Engine (M-series)
items.note: The NPU in every Apple SoC; the M4 announcement is the canonical spec source for its 38 TOPS on-device engine

items.name: Inferentia
items.note: Amazon's inference-side accelerator, the serving counterpart to Trainium

items.name: Trainium
items.note: Amazon's training chip; Trainium2 UltraServers underpin Anthropic's Project Rainier build-out

items.name: WSE-3
items.note: Wafer-scale engine: one 46,000mm2 die instead of a GPU cluster; 4 trillion transistors

items.name: TPU (Cloud TPU)
items.note: Google's in-house tensor processor family, from Trillium (v6e) onward; trains and serves Gemini and is rentable via Google Cloud

items.name: LPU
items.note: Deterministic single-core-style inference processor; the speed behind the Groq API tracked in the API directory

items.name: Maia 100
items.note: Azure's first in-house AI accelerator, announced with the Cobalt CPU for first-party workloads

reading.body:
Every major cloud provider and several specialists now maintain their own silicon, meaning the accelerator market is no longer a single-vendor story and the strategic logic of AI infrastructure has shifted toward custom hardware as a first-class capability.

The seven entries here divide into two broad groups. Apple's Neural Engine lives on-device, optimized for inference at the edge with a fixed power budget inside a mobile SoC. The rest target data-center workloads, and within that group there is a further split: training chips, inference chips, and designs that collapse that distinction. AWS separates the roles explicitly, with Trainium for training and Inferentia for serving. Google's TPU family does both, training and serving Gemini internally while also being rented externally. Cerebras approaches the problem from a different direction entirely, replacing a cluster of chips with a single wafer-scale die of 4 trillion transistors. Groq's LPU is designed around deterministic, high-throughput inference rather than training. Microsoft's Maia 100 is scoped to first-party Azure workloads.

The pattern matters for AI scaling because custom silicon is how operators reduce dependence on a single supplier, optimize the ratio of useful compute to power consumed, and control the economics of their own inference serving. Every chip in this list represents a building that had to be designed, a power budget that had to be allocated, and a supply chain that had to be secured before a single model ran on it. What this data does not cover is comparative performance across these chips, their relative energy draw, or how much capacity each deployment actually represents. Those gaps are significant: knowing that a chip exists is not the same as knowing whether it is a constraint or a surplus in the current infrastructure picture.
